name: Maidu, Southern dialect = Auburn Nisenan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Uldall, H. J. 1954. Maidu Phonetics. International Journal of American Linguistics 20(1): 8-16 [sketch written 1932; 'the Southern' dialect = Auburn (Hill) Nisenan]. Secondary: Shipley, William. 1961. Maidu and Nisenan: A Binary Survey. IJAL 27(1): 46-51.
catalog_locator: Uldall 1954, section 6 'Stress', pp. 13-14 (archive.org issue scan). Shipley 1961 pp. 46, 49.
catalog_quote: Stress does not seem to have any semantic or grammatical function, it has not been possible to find any pair of words distinguished by stress alone. No definite rule can be given as to the place of the stress in words and sentences, the best that can be done is to indicate tendencies. In nouns the stress normally falls on the last syllable even when the last syllable is a suffix: ki'le woman, potpo'to frog, hu:'k’-u-m chief (subj. case), hipiw-'di at the camp, but there are many exceptions such as 'maydik man, 'maydik-i-m, 'maydike, oko'peypey horned toad, which has a double stress with case-endings: oko'peype'y-i-m. In the verb the stress usually falls on the syllable immediately before the tense-suffix: ... he'nim-wesi (he) will talk, henim-'ti-wesi (he) will cause to talk, henim-ti-'men-wesi (he) will not cause to talk. In the present tense, however, the stress falls on the syllable containing the tense-suffix, [-m:] so'l-i-m (he) sings wa:'sa-m (he) kidnaps, wa:sa-me'n-i-m (he) doesn’t kidnap. ... Verbalizing suffixes on noun stems usually carry the stress: kile-'pe to marry, hi-'ya to make a house. Likewise nominalizing suffixes on verb stems: wo:nti-'hi the act of killing, siye:-'ma that which (was) made, tokis-'pe cook. An exception is -yu: 'tuy-yu bed, pa'yel-yu eating instrument. Imperative and subjunctive forms have the stress on the last syllable ... It would hardly be possible to go on listing rules and exceptions.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: via its text extracts and Uldall, H. J. 1954, 'Maidu Phonetics', IJAL 20(1): 8-16, archive.org issue scan, openly downloaded). Section 6 begins on printed p. 13 and runs onto p. 14 exactly as the locator says. The quoted passage is there word for word: 'Stress does not seem to have any semantic or grammatical function, it has not been possible to find any pair of words distinguished by stress alone. No definite rule can be given as to the place of the stress in words and sentences, the best that can be done is to indicate tendencies. In nouns the stress normally falls on the last syllable even when the last syllable is a suffix: ki'le woman, potpo'to frog, hu:'k'-u-m chief (su…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (realized as loudness plus higher pitch) is non-contrastive and, per the author, not rule-governed: nouns tend to be stressed on the final syllable (suffixes included) but with many lexical exceptions (e.g. initial-stressed 'maydik'); in verbs stress usually falls on the syllable immediately preceding the tense suffix, except that the present-tense suffix syllable itself takes the stress; derivational (verbalizing/nominalizing) suffixes usually attract stress; imperatives/subjunctives are final-stressed. Shipley 1961:49 adds that 'Stress is no longer phonemic in Nisenan' (Nisenan has phonemic length where Maidu has phonemic stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described as such; compound verbs may carry a stress on each stem or only on one (the latter more common), and some nouns show 'double stress' with case endings (oko'peype'y-i-m).
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns with non-final stress ('maydik man, 'maydik-i-m); present-tense forms stress the tense-suffix syllable; second-person subjunctive forms do not follow the final-stress rule; nominalizer -yu does not take stress ('tuy-yu bed); a stem may keep its stress when a derivative suffix intervenes (i'da:-'ti-t'omatoy). Author: 'It would hardly be possible to go on listing rules and exceptions.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: Uldall states the stress marks in his texts/grammar indicate word stress, not sentence stress; sentence stress is separately described as 'as irregular as word stress' (independent pronouns always stressed, preceding verb may lose its stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Uldall 1954 is titled 'Maidu Phonetics' but describes 'the Southern' dialect as opposed to 'the Northwestern' (p. 8-9), i.e. Southern Maidu = Nisenan; Shipley 1961 fn.1 states the data are 'H. J. Uldall's material on the Auburn dialect of Nisenan' and cites this paper as the published phonological statement 'For Nisenan', and Shipley 1956 fn.1 calls it 'Uldall's paper on the phonetics of Nisenan'. So the statement is for Auburn (Hill) Nisenan, fieldwork ca. 1930-32, glottocode nise1244 (no separate dialect code used). Eatough 1999 describes Central Hill Nisenan, a neighbouring Hill variety.

readall_conflicts: No new source-level conflict: the only listed work (Golla 2011, copy consulted) contributes nothing on stress because the copy is front matter only. The pre-existing tension in the record stands unchanged: the catalog record classes Auburn Nisenan stress as 'morphological' with an empty rule, while the one existing statement (Uldall 1954, IJAL 20(1) §6 'Stress', pp. 13-14) says no definite rule can be given for stress placement and that no minimal pairs exist, which the existing_statements entry reads as 'unclear or contradictory'.

sources.locator: Section 6 'Stress', pp. 13-14 (PDF pages 15-16 of the archive.org issue scan)
sources.note: Stress = loudness + higher pitch; not distinctive (no pair of words distinguished by stress alone); 'No definite rule can be given as to the place of the stress', only tendencies: nouns normally stress the last syllable (even a suffix) with many exceptions ('maydik); verbs usually stress the syllable immediately before the tense suffix, but the present-tense suffix syllable itself is stressed; verbalizing/nominalizing suffixes usually carry stress; imperatives/subjunctives final; sentence stress 'as irregular as word stress'; stress marks in his texts indicate word stress.

sources.citation: Shipley, William. 1961. Maidu and Nisenan: A Binary Survey. IJAL 27(1): 46-51.
sources.note: Comparative: 'All of the languages except Maidu have phonemic vowel length; the cognate Maidu forms usually (but not always) show phonemic stress' (p.46); 'Delayed stress does not occur in Nisenan' (p.48); 'Stress is no longer phonemic in Nisenan' (p.49). Fn.1 names Uldall 1954 as the published phonological statement for (Auburn) Nisenan and says the data are Uldall's Auburn-dialect Nisenan material.
